short: Hungary's royal army was destroyed in a night attack, and the kingdom lost much of its population.
full:
Béla IV had given asylum to the Cumans fleeing the steppe, which Batu treated as a casus belli. The Hungarian army — large, well armoured, and encumbered by a wagon fort — encamped near the Sajó River at Mohi on the night of 10 April 1241. Before dawn Subutai crossed the river downstream while Batu forced the bridge, and the two wings closed on the camp. Stone-throwers and, by some accounts, firecrackers were used to break the wagon line.

The Mongols left a deliberate gap in the encirclement. Men escaping through it strung themselves out across open country and were cut down over the following days; the archbishops of Esztergom and Kalocsa and much of the kingdom's nobility died there. Béla fled to an island off Dalmatia with a Mongol column behind him. Hungary was systematically stripped over the next year, with population losses plausibly between a fifth and a half in the worst-hit regions, until news of Ögedei's death took the army east in 1242. Béla returned and rebuilt in stone.
